## TL;DR

Expanded the Android Hub fixture QA sweep from its earlier 375px baseline to the requested 360px and 412px widths. The settings, add-server validation, edit-server sheet, offline fixture, and long-content checks passed in Chromium. No product layout bug was reproduced, so the only implementation change is the QA coverage. The documented run is browser evidence and does not verify a physical Android device or native biometric prompt.

## Work and rationale

I read the existing #1171 Android Hub fixture QA notes before running the app. That report already described the long-name flex sizing fix and the overflow wrapping rules, so this pass focused on the additional widths and states requested by #1182. I used the app's own Vite server and fixture query parameters rather than changing application code to synthesize screenshots.

The first Vite start could not resolve the Capacitor imports because the mobile package's dependencies were not installed in the mobile package context. I installed its declared dependencies with Bun, restarted the server, and confirmed the app could then load in the Playwright sweep. This was a local dependency setup step; no dependency declarations or lockfiles were changed intentionally.

I updated `mobile/scripts/fixture-qa.ts` to sweep the seven supported fixture states at 360px and 412px. For each fixture it checks element bounds and clean page/console state. I added lock settings interaction checks that remove the stored `repoos.lock` setting before toggling, ensuring both width runs start disabled even if a prior run persisted a choice. I also exercised the edit sheet with the long path URL and submitted the invalid HTTP URL at both widths. The existing no-breakpoint URL, long picker name, discovery error text, warning, and update-note checks remain in the sweep.

I wrote `docs/qa/2026-11-android-hub-second-pass.md` with the setup, measurement method, results, findings, and device-QA boundary. It states that no CSS bug was reproduced and does not present browser observations as Android device evidence. The final fixture run passed 47/47 checks, and the mobile typecheck and production build passed. The required `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed remote scoped build and tests, formatting, lint, branch-artifact validation, and UI smoke.

## Approaches tried

I first attempted to use the browser automation surface, but the browser host was unavailable in this session. The repository already had a Playwright-based fixture QA script, so I used that direct harness for deterministic viewport, interaction, and overflow checks. The harness starts Chromium at device scale factor 2 and tests actual app routes, using the existing fixtures for reachable, empty, offline, settings, add, and discovery states.

The first expanded run exposed two shortcomings in my initial test assertion: it expected the unsupported-device note even though Chromium reports the biometric plugin interface as supported, and it clicked the toggle unconditionally, which could switch off a preference persisted by the previous width pass. I removed the unsupported-device assumption and made the settings interaction state-aware: the script checks `aria-checked`, toggles only when needed, then waits for the scope selector. This keeps the check centered on the visible control and geometry rather than plugin capability or run order.

## Challenges and blockers

There was no reproducible product defect to fix in the exercised browser states. The run cannot trigger or validate a genuine native biometric prompt in desktop Chromium. The fixture-based offline state represents the Hub's unreachable server row; it does not make a real network request. The UI browser automation host was unavailable, and the script does not produce visual screenshot artifacts, so this report relies on the script's measured bounds and visible DOM state rather than retained screenshots.

The QA script and app run on this host. Physical Android device verification remains outside the evidence collected in this session. In particular, a native WebView can differ in keyboard insets, safe-area behavior, touch interaction, and system biometric UI.

## Key learnings

The prior 375px checks were useful but left the requested narrow and wider phone widths unguarded. Running the same geometry checks at both widths is inexpensive enough to keep in the existing sweep. Persistent preferences can also make UI automation order-dependent; reading the actual switch state before acting avoids toggling the setting off accidentally. Finally, capability signals from a browser shim are not equivalent to device support, so the test should assert the intended screen controls rather than an environment-specific unsupported warning.
